title: The bow that threw kings
hookLine: kings line up for a bow almost no one can bend, and their crowns hit the floor
carry: ahamkara, the ego, is what falls
tomorrow: why does Karna put down the bow?

cards: The arena at Panchala is packed. Kings and princes have come from far and wide, dressed in their best. Brahmins have come to watch.
There's music, and the noise of a crowd that has waited for this. Somewhere among the brahmins sit five brothers in borrowed clothes, whom everyone here believes are dead.
Then Draupadi enters, carrying a garland, and her brother Dhrishtadyumna rises to announce the terms.

teach.b: Here's the challenge, in paraphrase. This is the bow, these are the arrows. Up high is a mark, and in front of it a device set in the air, with an opening in it.
Whoever strings the bow, shoots through the opening and hits the mark, and is worthy in birth and form and strength, wins my sister. Now a detail the text gives.

teach.h: A STIFF BOW; THE KINGS FALL.
teach.b: Drupada had hoped all along to give his daughter to Arjuna, so he had this bow made so stiff that hardly anyone could string it. One by one, the kings try, and the bow beats them. Some can't bend it at all.
Some get close, and it springs back and throws them to the ground, their crowns and ornaments scattered across the floor. Great names, humbled in front of everyone.

Hindu teachers have a word for what hits the floor with those crowns: ahamkara, the ego, literally the I-maker. It's the part of us that says: I'm the one doing this, I deserve this, everyone is watching me.
In the Gita, Krishna says the self confused by ahamkara thinks, I am the doer, when it's nature's forces doing the work. Hinduism doesn't ask you to stop acting.
It asks you to act without that swelling I. Many tellers read the swayamvara this way: kings who walked up sure of their own names, thrown down by a bow that didn't care who they were.
Tomorrow, someone very different walks up to the bow.

how: The contest at Panchala, with the bow and the mark, is shown in Hindu painting, dance and storytelling; in some retellings the archer aims at a fish's eye seen reflected in water below.

o: a test of birth, so only kings may enter the arena
a contest where kings fight each other for a bride
a princess's choosing, here run through a hard bow test

s: the kings strung the bow easily
some couldn't bend it; some were thrown to the ground by it.
Drupada had hoped Arjuna would win
the text says he'd wanted to give his daughter to Arjuna all along.
Hinduism teaches you to stop acting so the ego cannot grow
the Gita asks you to act, without the ahamkara that says 'I am the doer'.

games.q: a friend says: those kings just lost a contest. why would a Hindu teacher bring up the ego? what fits?
o: they walked up sure of their own names; ahamkara, the I-maker, is what hit the floor with their crowns.
because losing is shameful, so you shouldn't compete at all.
because the bow was cursed, so ego has nothing to do with it.
games.why: many tellers read the scattered crowns as ahamkara humbled. Hinduism doesn't say don't try; it says act without the swelling I.

practice: Fold your hands at your chest, the way Hindus greet each other and the gods with namaste, and bow your head a little. Bring to mind one place where you badly want to be seen as the best: a class, a team, a group chat.
With each breath out, set a little of that I down, the way you'd set down a heavy bag. If you pray, offer the work to God and let go of the credit.
If you don't, just notice how much lighter the work feels without the crowd watching.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi's swayamvara. A bow almost no one could bend, a mark beyond a device set high in the air, and kings thrown to the floor.

orig.note: Sanskrit ahaṃkāra: the ego, literally the I-maker; the part that says 'I am the doer'.

carryVoice: Your line: ahamkara, the ego, is what falls. Crowns on the floor at Panchala. Day seven hundred forty-one.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Swayamvara Parva (the arena; Dhrishtadyumna announces the terms; the bow and the mark; the kings fail)
Bhagavad Gita 3.27 (Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva): actions are done by nature's qualities, but the self deluded by ahamkara thinks 'I am the doer'
